tagline: A river road links Coast Range forests with Alsea Falls
intro: The South Fork-Alsea River Back Country Byway follows a river of rapids and pools through Oregon’s Coast Range. The Federal Highway Administration gives a driving time of 30 minutes and highlights riverside recreation and the forested hills. BLM identifies the road as a National Back Country Byway, lined by forests in different stages of growth. Near Alsea Falls, old-growth Douglas fir and western red cedar occupy the ridges, while younger firs and vine maples grow at the recreation site. Spring and summer bring wildflowers to the fields along the route, including columbine, foxglove and larkspur. The river parallels the road, with places for picnicking, hiking and camping at the BLM recreation site.

Logging was once Alsea’s main industry. Farther along the corridor, Glenbrook grew around a sawmill established in 1919, with a logging railway built into the surrounding forest. By 2024, little remained of Glenbrook beyond the mill pond.

From Alsea, head south on Alsea-Deadwood Highway to South Fork Road, then follow the paved road to the falls. The river drops 30 feet in the day-use area. South Fork Road connects with Alpine Road; Glenbrook lies along Alpine Road west of Alpine, which is west of Monroe.

moments.title: Alsea
moments.text: Near Alsea, the North and South Forks join to form the Alsea River. The community stands on Oregon Route 34 beside the river. Settlers arrived from the Willamette Valley in the early 1850s to take up donation land claims. Logging became its principal industry; it is now known for fishing, particularly steelhead. West of town, Hayden Bridge carries Hayden Road across the river. The covered span was built in 1918 and later rebuilt with larger portals to accommodate bigger vehicles. Narrow openings beneath its side-wall eaves admit light to the interior.

moments.title: Alsea Falls
moments.text: The South Fork drops 30 feet at Alsea Falls, within the recreation site’s day-use area. Trails wind through the surrounding forest to picnic grounds and beyond. The forest has different ages: younger Douglas fir and vine maple grow at the site, while old-growth fir and western red cedar stand on nearby ridges. BLM’s day-use bridge provides a view of the falls. Green Peak Falls, a separate 45-foot waterfall, is reached by road or trail through the private campground at McBee Park. The recreation site lies in Benton County, 13 miles west of Monroe in the Oregon Coast Range.

moments.title: Alpine
moments.text: Alpine’s school had a name before there was a settlement to share it. The community took the school’s name, referring to its position atop a foothill of the Central Oregon Coast Range. In 1908, the Corvallis and Alsea River Railway Company began a line that stopped at Alpine when its funding ran out. A post office followed in 1912 and operated until 1976; Alpine now uses a Monroe mailing address. Alpine Elementary School closed in 2003. The community has burned three times since its early-twentieth-century heyday.
